title: On Optimizing Route-Responsive Urban Tree Placement in City-Scale Pedestrian Networks

problem.claim: Select k urban tree planting sites to maximize pedestrians' expected utility under random origin–destination demand and utility-maximizing path choice.

gap.claim: Urban tree siting is comparatively less explored from an algorithmic optimization perspective.

contributions.claim: Introduces a shade-aware modeling framework and formulates the Route-responsive Urban Tree Optimization problem.
Shows that the non-submodular RUTO objective admits submodular upper and lower bounds capturing its max-coverage structure.
Instantiates a sandwich approximation framework with solution-dependent approximation guarantees and proposes faster proxy objectives without formal guarantees.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on synthetic grids and real-world pedestrian networks report that the sandwich-approximation algorithms and proxy heuristics match a direct greedy baseline in objective value.
The authors report that the sandwich-approximation algorithms and proxy heuristics are up to two orders of magnitude faster than the direct greedy baseline.

narrative_sequence.summary: Positions urban tree siting as underexplored as an algorithmic optimization problem.
Defines shade-aware route-responsive tree placement as selecting k sites to maximize expected pedestrian utility.
Identifies the induced route responses and bilevel structure, along with the non-submodular objective.
Uses submodular bounds for sandwich approximation and introduces faster proxy heuristics.
Reports comparable objective values to direct greedy with substantially lower runtime on synthetic and real-world networks.

source_observation.claim: A difficult bilevel, non-submodular placement problem is addressed through submodular upper and lower bounds.

interpretation.claim: Bounding a hard objective may enable approximation methods with explicit guarantees.

application.claim: For route-responsive infrastructure placement, consider bound-based approximation before relying only on direct greedy search.

exception.claim: Proxy objectives may be faster but do not provide formal guarantees.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the utility function, demand distribution, or route-choice details.
The abstract does not quantify the approximation guarantees or experimental settings.
